questions.q: The true label is Cat (one-hot $P = [1, 0, 0]$) and the model predicts $Q = [0.25,\ 0.5,\ 0.25]$. What is $H(P, Q)$ in bits?
questions.explain: With a one-hot target the sum collapses to one term: $-\log_2 Q(\text{Cat}) = -\log_2 0.25 = 2$ bits. $1$ bit is the surprise of the (wrong) Dog prediction; $1.5$ bits is the entropy of $Q$, not the cross-entropy.

questions.q: Gibbs' inequality says $H(P, Q) \ge H(P)$. What is the gap $H(P, Q) - H(P)$?
options: The KL divergence $D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)$, which is $0$ only when $Q = P$
The surprise of the most likely class
questions.explain: $H(P, Q) = H(P) + D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)$: the inevitable entropy of reality plus the 'coding waste' of using $Q$. The waste vanishes exactly at $Q = P$ (the 🎯 Perfect Fit preset).

questions.q: With softmax outputs $Q = [0.7,\ 0.2,\ 0.1]$ and target $P = [1, 0, 0]$, what is the gradient $\partial H_{\text{nats}} / \partial z$ with respect to the logits?
questions.explain: For softmax + cross-entropy (in nats) the gradient is simply $Q - P$: prediction minus reality. The log cancels the softmax's exp, so the gradient does not saturate even when the model is confidently wrong. (In bits it is the same vector divided by $\ln 2$.)

questions.q: With label smoothing, the target is $P = [0.90,\ 0.05,\ 0.05]$. Which prediction $Q$ minimizes the cross-entropy?
questions.explain: Cross-entropy is minimized at $Q = P$. Pushing to $[1, 0, 0]$ assigns $\approx 0$ probability to classes with $P > 0$, so the loss blows up; that is exactly how label smoothing discourages 100% confidence.
